resources.string: Android asks you in a pop-up the first time the app needs it. You can revoke it at any time: Settings > Apps > the app > Permissions.
It is never granted with a single tap: you have to choose “Allow all the time” in the app\'s permissions. Switch it back to “Allow only while using the app” if in doubt.
No separate prompt: it comes with access to your photos and videos. Removing the app\'s photo access removes it too.
A powerful access you have to switch on yourself in a dedicated settings screen (Settings > Apps > Special app access). An app that sends you there needs a very good reason.
It is granted automatically at install time, without any prompt, and cannot be revoked without uninstalling the app.
Know your location even when the app is closed or you are not using it.

This is round-the-clock tracking: home, work, places of care, worship or dating, schedules… A few days of locations are enough to identify you and reconstruct your life. This data is highly sought after by data brokers.
Know your location to within a few metres while you use the app.
Essential for a GPS or a running app, but it reveals exactly where you are. For an app that only needs the city (weather, shop), approximate location is enough.
Know your location at neighbourhood or city level.
Less intrusive than GPS, it still reveals your regular movements and is often used to target local advertising.
Read the GPS coordinates stored in your photos and videos.
Your photos tell where you were and when: home, holidays, places you visit. An app can retrace your past movements without ever asking for your location.
Read all your text messages, old and new.
Your private conversations, but also banking and login verification codes received by SMS: enough to take over accounts. Google restricts it to default SMS apps.
Be notified of and read each text message as it arrives.
Lets an app intercept one-time codes as soon as they arrive, a classic technique of banking malware.
Send text messages on your behalf, without going through your messaging app.
Risk of premium-rate texts billed to your plan, or messages sent to your contacts without your knowledge.
Receive and read MMS (messages with a photo or video).
Gives access to the content of private messages, photos included.
Read the list of your calls: numbers, dates, durations.
Who you call, when and for how long maps out your personal, medical or professional circle. Google restricts it to default phone apps.
Add, change or delete entries in your call history.
An app could erase the trace of calls it made or tamper with your history.
See the number you dial and redirect or cancel the call (legacy permission, removed since Android 10).
Reveals every number you call; its presence often betrays an old or poorly maintained app.
Call a number directly, without you confirming in the Phone app.
Useful for a “call customer service” button, but also allows calls to premium-rate numbers.
Pick up or hang up an incoming call for you.
Legitimate for a watch or a connected car; elsewhere, an app has no reason to handle your calls.
Know whether you are on a call, your carrier, your network and information about the SIM card.
The reassuring name hides information useful for recognising you from one app to another. Advertising SDKs love it to build a device fingerprint.
Read the phone number of your SIM cards.
Your number is a stable, personal identifier that can be used to find you elsewhere (messaging apps, data leaks, cold calling).
Read all your contacts: names, numbers, e-mails, addresses, notes.
This is not only your data but your loved ones\' too, and they agreed to nothing. Address books are often uploaded to servers to “find friends” or feed profiles.
An app can add its own entries (sales number, support) or alter yours.
See the accounts registered on the phone (Google, e-mail, social networks).
Since Android 8, the app only sees its own accounts or those you entrust to it, but asking for it still signals interest in your online identity.
Record sound through the microphone while you use the app.
Conversations, voices, background noise: the microphone picks up far more than your voice command. Android shows a green dot when it is in use; be wary if it appears for no reason.
Take photos and videos, or scan a code, while you use the app.
Normal for scanning a QR code or a document. Less so for an app with nothing to photograph. A green dot signals when it is in use.
Read all your appointments and those of shared calendars.
Your medical, work or personal appointments, with places and attendees, describe your life precisely, and that of the other guests.
Handy for adding a booking, but an app can also delete or change your appointments.
Read health sensors: heart rate, blood oxygen, etc.
Health data is among the most sensitive there is (GDPR, article 9): it can reveal illness, stress or pregnancy.
Read your health sensors even when the app is not open.
Permanent health monitoring, rarely needed outside a watch or medical tracking app.
Detect whether you are walking, running, cycling or driving, and count your steps.
Reveals your habits, journeys and lifestyle, even without access to your location.
Read the photos, videos, music and documents in shared storage.
Opens access to your whole gallery and downloads. Since Android 13 it has been replaced by finer-grained access: VYLIA only counts it for apps built for older versions.
Read, modify and delete every file in shared storage, without restriction.
ID documents, statements, photos, backups: everything becomes readable. In principle reserved for file managers and antivirus apps.
Read the photos in your gallery.
Faces, photographed documents, screenshots, places: a gallery says a lot. Android 14 lets you share only selected photos; prefer that option.
Read the videos in your gallery.
Same concern as photos: your videos show people and places.
Read your music, podcasts and recordings.
Not very sensitive for music, more so for voice memos or call recordings.
Detect Bluetooth devices around you (earbuds, watches, beacons).
Bluetooth beacons in shops and public places reveal where you are, even without location access.
Detect and connect to nearby Wi-Fi devices (printer, speaker, camera).
The list of nearby networks and devices can be used to infer your location.
See the full list of apps installed on your phone.

Your app list says a lot about you: a health, banking, dating, religious or political app reveals intimate information. The combination of installed apps is also a near-unique fingerprint for tracking you.
Know which apps you use, when and for how long.
Your sleeping hours, habits and night-time or work usage can be read in these statistics.
Offer to install apps downloaded outside the Play Store.
A gateway for apps not checked by Google, or even malicious ones. Legitimate for a browser or an alternative store (F-Droid), suspicious elsewhere.
Read everything shown on screen and act for you: tap, type text, navigate.

This is Android\'s most powerful access, designed to help people with disabilities. It can read passwords and messages, and it is the favourite tool of spyware. Only grant it to an accessibility app you trust.
Read all your notifications, from every app, and dismiss them.
Message previews, e-mails, verification codes, bank alerts: everything goes through notifications.
Lock the phone, enforce a PIN, wipe all data, prevent uninstallation.
Legitimate for a work phone managed by your employer or an anti-theft app. Elsewhere it is excessive control, sometimes used to make an app impossible to remove.
Show windows on top of other apps (chat bubbles, floating player).
A fake window can cover a real app to make you type a password or tap a button without realising.

Collects your phone\'s advertising ID, your interests and how you react to ads, then auctions them to many advertisers every time an ad is shown. Your data thus travels to dozens of companies you have never heard of.
Builds a detailed portrait of you: habits, purchases, interests, sometimes health or opinions inferred from your behaviour. These profiles are cross-referenced between apps and feed data brokers.
Records your locations, often continuously, including through Bluetooth beacons in shops. They reveal home, work and sensitive places (health, worship, dating) and are almost impossible to anonymise.
Links your activity to an identity: Facebook or other account, device identifier. It becomes possible to recognise you from one app to another and tie your usage to your real name.

Measures what you do in the app (screens viewed, taps, purchases, time spent) and sends it to a third party, often Google or Facebook, even if you have no account there. Also used to attribute your install to an ad campaign.
Sends a technical report when the app crashes: phone model, Android version, steps before the error. Useful for app quality and not very intrusive, but it still describes your device.
The Exodus database does not document what it does. To be safe, it is counted as an analytics tracker.
Unknown category: no permission is presumed necessary, each one is considered unexpected.
Guidance relies on your location. Microphone (voice commands), contacts (addresses) and Bluetooth (car) are tolerated.
Timetables and routes around you. The camera (scanning a ticket) and calendar (adding a trip) are tolerated.
Locate the car and connect to it over Bluetooth. Contacts, calendar and microphone are tolerated for in-car features.
The city is enough for local weather. Precise or background location is only tolerated, for alerts.
A torch, calculator or compass needs nothing sensitive. The camera is tolerated for the torch, even though Android has not needed it since version 6.
Write to your contacts, send photos, videos and voice messages, make calls.
Find recipients and attach files or photos. Calendar and microphone are tolerated.
Post photos, videos and sounds. Finding friends and tagging a post\'s location are only tolerated.
Play your music and videos. Bluetooth (speakers) and microphone (music recognition) are tolerated.
Reading articles requires no sensitive permission. The city is tolerated for local news.
Scan a product and photograph a listing. Location, to find a nearby shop or listing, is tolerated.
Scan a cheque or an ID document. Reading your SMS is unnecessary: Android passes on verification codes without giving access to them.
Send a prescription or a receipt as a photo. Calendar and location are tolerated for appointments.
Pair and sync the watch: Bluetooth, sensors, activity, location. SMS and calls are tolerated to show them on your wrist.
Track your routes and efforts: location, activity, sensors, Bluetooth for a heart-rate strap.
Scan a QR code to add an account. Accessibility is tolerated for password autofill.
A browser asks nothing for itself: it relays requests from websites (camera, microphone, location), hence a simple tolerance.
Talk to the assistant and show it pictures. Calendar, contacts and location are only tolerated.
Open, scan and sync your files and photos.
Take and manage your photos and videos, connect to a camera over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi.
Find places and events around you. Calendar and photos are tolerated for bookings.
A game needs no sensitive permission. Microphone and Bluetooth are tolerated for voice chat and controllers.
Reading the screen and acting for you is precisely their job: accessibility and microphone are justified.
Send homework or documents as photos. The calendar is tolerated for the timetable.
Average user app score of at least 80/100
